text: Some years later he secured an excellent post in Petersburg, and, delighted with his rising fortunes, he threw himself into decorating a new house exactly as people of his rank were expected to. <break time="0.8s" /> One day, climbing a stepladder to show an upholsterer how he wanted the curtains hung, he slipped and struck his side against the handle of the window frame, though the bruise seemed trivial at the time. <break time="0.8s" /> Soon afterward, however, he began to notice a strange taste in his mouth and a dull pressure in his side, which neither rest nor medicine nor the passing weeks could drive away. <break time="0.8s" /> The famous doctor he consulted behaved exactly as Ivan Ilyich himself behaved in court, treating the case as a puzzle about a kidney or an appendix rather than as a question of whether his patient would live. <break time="0.8s" /> At home his complaints only irritated his wife and daughter, who considered his illness an inconvenience, almost a fault, as though he were suffering on purpose to spoil their busy social lives. <break time="0.8s" /> Long ago he had learned the logic lesson that Caius is a man, that all men are mortal, and that Caius is therefore mortal, and it had always seemed perfectly correct as applied to Caius. <break time="0.8s" /> He, however, had never been Caius or any abstract man but little Vanya, with a mother and a father, with toys and a striped leather ball, and for such a being to die seemed impossible. <break time="0.8s" /> He tried to push the thought away by returning to his work, yet in the middle of a trial it would quietly appear again, standing before him and looking straight into his eyes.
